strategy_title: Develop a rigorous framework for measuring AI agent reliability
strategy_text: Investigate how autonomous and semi-autonomous AI agents can be measured objectively, reproducibly, and meaningfully across diverse tasks and operating conditions. Build an evaluation framework that distinguishes superficial task completion from correctness, robustness, and dependable behavior. Audit representative agent benchmarks for task-selection effects, environmental variability, evaluator bias, contamination, and weak completion oracles. Define operational measures for end-to-end success, partial completion, error severity, recovery, repeat-trial consistency, tool-use correctness, and resources per successful outcome. Specify how to evaluate stochastic agents, long dependency chains, long-running tasks, external tools, and changing environments. Propose repeated-trial protocols, uncertainty intervals, failure-distribution reporting, and comparisons under controlled compute, time, tool, and monetary budgets. State the evidence and replication needed for defensible reliability claims; separate benchmark-specific gains from general improvements. Deliver a protocol with task strata, outcome rubrics, baseline comparisons, statistical analysis, and explicit limits on what its results can establish.

strategy_runs.strategy_title: Understand failure propagation and recovery in autonomous AI agents
strategy_runs.strategy_text: Map how agents fail during extended, multi-step tasks and determine which failures are detectable, recoverable, or silently corrupt later results. Examine incorrect reasoning and plans, tool misuse, incomplete observations, stale or compressed context, instruction misunderstandings, environmental changes, and accumulated state errors. Trace concrete failure chains from initiating fault through subsequent actions to user-visible consequences; distinguish model limitations from architecture, orchestration, memory, interface, and environment failures. Investigate detection of silent errors, calibrated uncertainty versus actual failure, retry and replanning policies, escalation, and safe termination. Analyze checkpointing, state reconstruction, independent verification, rollback, idempotency, and human intervention as recovery mechanisms. For each mechanism, specify assumptions, failure modes, and measurable recovery criteria; compare recovery against restarting and continuing without intervention. Develop fault-injection scenarios and trace-based analyses that reveal propagation and test whether recovery restores correct state rather than merely producing a plausible answer. Deliver a failure taxonomy, causal workflow maps, and a prioritized set of falsifiable experiments, distinguishing observed evidence from proposed mechanisms.

strategy_snapshot.title: Develop a rigorous framework for measuring AI agent reliability
Understand failure propagation and recovery in autonomous AI agents
Test architectural mechanisms for dependable agent outcomes

problem:
Autonomous AI agents are increasingly expected to complete complex tasks involving planning, reasoning, external tools, persistent state, and interaction with changing environments. Demonstrations and benchmark results show that agents can perform many such tasks, but provide limited evidence that they remain dependable across repeated executions, unfamiliar conditions, long-running workflows, and settings where mistakes have significant consequences. This project asks how autonomous and semi-autonomous agents can be evaluated and engineered to deliver reliable, correct, recoverable, and reproducible results across extended, multi-step tasks.

Agent reliability is a system-level property. Probabilistic decisions, dynamically constructed plans, incomplete observations, tool interfaces, memory, orchestration, and external state all affect whether the intended outcome is actually achieved. Small errors can propagate through later actions and yield plausible but incorrect results. An agent may claim completion without satisfying the task, recover from one failure while introducing another, or behave differently across otherwise comparable runs. Reliability therefore cannot be inferred from fluent explanations, a single successful trajectory, agreement among similar models, or benchmark scores alone.

Investigate three connected questions. First, how should reliability be defined and measured so evaluation reflects actual correctness, robustness, consistency, recoverability, tool-use quality, and cost rather than superficial completion? Second, what are the principal sources of failure, how do errors propagate through multi-step execution, and which signals and interventions can detect, contain, or recover from failures without creating additional risks? Third, which engineering mechanisms demonstrably improve outcomes, and how can their effects be established through controlled experiments rather than architectural intuition or anecdotal success? The strategies approach these questions from complementary measurement, failure-analysis, and intervention perspectives; none presumes a preferred architecture.

Use available research literature, software-reliability principles, empirical evaluation methods, and documented agent-system designs. Examine the relationship between model capability and end-to-end system reliability, including tool interfaces, state management, verification, orchestration, uncertainty handling, changing environments, recovery, and execution budgets. Assess benchmark sensitivity to task selection, evaluator bias, contamination, and weak completion oracles. Consider stochastic behavior, repeated trials, long dependency chains, held-out tasks, fault injection, independent correctness judgments, and uncertainty in estimated success rates. Where comparisons are proposed, make assumptions and controls explicit, including model and prompt versions, task difficulty, environment, tool access, compute, latency, and monetary budgets.

Evaluate competing approaches on the strength and limits of their evidence. Distinguish measured results from formal or theoretical arguments, proposed mechanisms, and unsupported claims; do not present planned experiments as completed or infer causal benefit from correlation. Account for correlated errors among agents or critics that share models and training data, and for the difficulty of constructing an independent oracle for open-ended tasks. Analyze tradeoffs among reliability, flexibility, recovery overhead, latency, and computational expense, including cases where a safeguard shifts rather than removes risk.

The intended outcome is an evidence-grounded account of what reliability claims current evaluations can support, a practical and reproducible evaluation framework, a causal taxonomy of important failure and recovery modes, and architectural principles whose limits are explicit. Identify unresolved questions and specify discriminating experiments needed to validate competing claims. The project is open-ended: conclusions should remain proportional to the quality, independence, and generality of available evidence.

output.claim: Conditional on a fixed finite evaluation cohort, a predeclared binary correctness rubric at observation horizon H, and accurate reference-label audits sampled uniformly within evaluator-acceptance cells, true cohort correctness can be bounded without assuming independent agent runs. Acceptance rates alone cannot identify even the direction of a correctness difference between agents: repeated evaluation can estimate a systematically misleading acceptance rate arbitrarily precisely.
output.method: Use an exact binary-label decomposition, an observationally indistinguishable counterexample, and a finite-population audit protocol. The competing explanations are that an acceptance gain reflects greater correctness or instead greater evaluator false acceptance. Auditing both accepted and rejected outputs distinguishes these explanations through their different reference-label error rates. The derivation concerns a fixed cohort, not deployment generalization; it assumes a trustworthy correctness oracle for the audited records. No computation or empirical benchmark was executed because both supplied runtimes are unavailable.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the evaluation unit and target before scoring
reasoning_steps.argument: For each agent a, freeze a cohort of N_a task executions, including assigned tasks, environment versions, tool access, model and prompt versions, execution budgets, and observation horizon H. Let O_ai be the evaluator's binary acceptance decision. Let Y_ai be reference correctness: the required external postcondition holds at H and all predeclared safety and resource constraints are satisfied. Timeouts and missing required evidence count as failures under this rubric, not discarded runs. Define q_a = N_a^(-1) sum_i O_ai and p_a = N_a^(-1) sum_i Y_ai. These are finite-cohort rates. Correlation among executions does not invalidate their definitions. The binary target should accompany, not replace, separate severity, cost, and recovery reporting.

reasoning_steps.title: Acceptance and correctness differ by two identifiable error components
reasoning_steps.argument: Define f_a = N_a^(-1) sum_i O_ai(1-Y_ai), the fraction of all runs falsely accepted, and n_a = N_a^(-1) sum_i (1-O_ai)Y_ai, the fraction falsely rejected. The pointwise identity Y = O - O(1-Y) + (1-O)Y gives p_a = q_a - f_a + n_a exactly. Therefore p_A-p_B = q_A-q_B-f_A+f_B+n_A-n_B. An acceptance gain can arise from a correctness gain, increased false acceptance, decreased false rejection, or a combination; acceptance alone cannot separate these terms.

reasoning_steps.title: Exact ranking reversal with unchanged evaluator observations
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider 100 equally weighted records per agent, indexed i=1,...,100. Fix O_Ai=1 exactly when i<=90 and O_Bi=1 exactly when i<=80. In World I, set Y_Ai=O_Ai and Y_Bi=O_Bi: correctness is 90% versus 80%. In World II, set Y_Ai=1 exactly when i<=70, leaving Y_Bi=O_Bi: correctness is 70% versus 80%. All observed acceptance labels are identical across worlds; in World II, A has 20 false acceptances and no false rejections. If indices are instead sampled uniformly with replacement, both worlds also induce the same distribution of observed label pairs for every sample size. Thus no estimator using only these observations can consistently distinguish the opposite correctness rankings. Other logs do not help if they omit the distinguishing external reference state; this construction does not claim impossibility when logs actually determine correctness.

reasoning_steps.title: Sharp bounds when evaluator disagreement is bounded
reasoning_steps.argument: Suppose an externally justified bound states that P(O_a != Y_a)<=epsilon_a for a uniformly selected cohort record. Since |p_a-q_a|=|n_a-f_a|<=n_a+f_a, p_a lies in [L_a,U_a]=[max(0,q_a-epsilon_a), min(1,q_a+epsilon_a)]. These bounds are sharp in the unrestricted binary-label model: the lower endpoint is attained by changing min(epsilon_a,q_a) accepted mass into incorrect outcomes, and the upper endpoint by changing min(epsilon_a,1-q_a) rejected mass into correct outcomes. On a finite cohort, use attainable integer counts. Consequently the unrestricted difference interval is [L_A-U_B,U_A-L_B], with both endpoints attainable absent further cross-agent constraints. Strict superiority is certified only if L_A>U_B; a simple sufficient condition is q_A-q_B>epsilon_A+epsilon_B. The inequality is a certificate under a validated error bound, not a reason to assume that bound.

reasoning_steps.title: Estimate the needed errors by auditing both acceptance cells
reasoning_steps.argument: Within each agent, partition the fixed records by O=1 and O=0. Let r_a+ be the fraction with Y=0 in the accepted cell and r_a- the fraction with Y=1 in the rejected cell. Then f_a=q_a r_a+, n_a=(1-q_a)r_a-, and p_a=q_a(1-r_a+)+(1-q_a)r_a-. Uniformly sample records without replacement separately within every nonempty cell, and obtain reference labels independently of the agent's completion claim. An accepted-only audit identifies false acceptance but leaves false rejection unknown. Auditing both cells identifies both terms if the reference labels are accurate. An empty cell has zero weight, so its conditional error rate need not be defined.

reasoning_steps.title: A simultaneous finite-cohort confidence certificate
reasoning_steps.argument: Let K<=4 be the number of nonempty agent-by-acceptance cells for two agents. Prespecify each audit sample size m_c. For a nonexhaustively audited cell, compute its observed binary error fraction rhat_c and t_c=sqrt(log(2K/alpha)/(2m_c)); set l_c=max(0,rhat_c-t_c), u_c=min(1,rhat_c+t_c). Hoeffding's inequality for uniform sampling without replacement bounds each cell's two-sided failure probability by 2 exp(-2m_c t_c^2)=alpha/K. For an exhaustively audited cell set l_c=u_c to its exact error fraction. The union bound gives simultaneous coverage at least 1-alpha, without independence between cells or between agent runs. On that event, P_a_lower=q_a(1-u_a+)+(1-q_a)l_a- and P_a_upper=q_a(1-l_a+)+(1-q_a)u_a- bound p_a. Omit zero-weight cells. Hence p_A-p_B is covered by [P_A_lower-P_B_upper, P_A_upper-P_B_lower]. Positive lower endpoint certifies a cohort advantage; an interval crossing zero is inconclusive, not equivalence.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify the discriminating observation and its failure modes
reasoning_steps.argument: For the exact counterexample, a complete audit of A's accepted cell yields r_A+=0 in World I and 20/90=2/9 in World II; all other cell errors are zero. Substitution gives p_A=0.9 in World I and p_A=0.9(1-2/9)=0.7 in World II, while p_B=0.8 in both. A feasible empirical version freezes outputs first, draws prespecified random audits, blinds adjudicators to agent identity where possible, and checks external postconditions such as authoritative final state rather than merely replaying completion text. Partial audits may remain inconclusive. Agreement between two critics sharing blind spots is not an accurate-reference guarantee. Delayed failures beyond H, inaccessible side effects, and ambiguous rubrics can invalidate the target or oracle premise.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate oracle uncertainty from generalization and causal claims
reasoning_steps.argument: The audit interval concerns the realized cohort only: even perfectly recovering every Y_ai does not establish performance on new tasks, changing environments, or longer horizons. A subsequent mechanism comparison should use held-out task strata, paired task/environment conditions, randomized treatment assignment where feasible, and explicit budget matching. Repeated seeds within a task cannot substitute for new tasks when estimating deployment generality. A frozen-cohort audit can diagnose a misleading benchmark gain, but cannot by itself show that a safeguard caused better deployment outcomes. The result here is a standard measurement-error argument specialized into a practical agent-evaluation certificate; literature novelty and empirical usefulness have not been assessed.

assumptions: The target is a fixed, fully recorded finite cohort with prespecified execution constraints and observation horizon H; its binary reference correctness labels are well-defined and stable.
Reference-label audits correctly recover the prescribed external correctness labels, rather than merely agreeing with the original evaluator.
For the confidence certificate, audit sample sizes are fixed in advance and records are sampled uniformly without replacement within each nonempty agent-by-acceptance cell.
output.evidence_status: Analytical partial result: an explicit ranking-reversal counterexample and a finite-cohort audit certificate are derived. No benchmark, external source inspection, runtime execution, or independent verification occurred; deployment generality and the accuracy of practical reference oracles remain untested.
open_obligations: Instantiate the protocol on a documented agent benchmark and inspect its actual scoring code, task sampling, outcome horizon, and external-state records; none were supplied here.
Validate the reference-label process on the chosen domain, including hidden side effects, delayed failures, adjudication disagreement, and the possibility of shared evaluator blind spots.
Execute a prespecified two-cell audit to measure whether an observed acceptance advantage survives correction; the constructed example is not an observed agent result.

Extend from finite-cohort certification to deployment estimates using explicit task/environment sampling, task-level dependence handling, held-out conditions, and uncertainty for those sampling stages.
Evaluate recovery, error severity, tool-use quality, and resource tradeoffs separately; this binary correctness result does not establish improvements on those objectives.

output.claim: Under an explicitly observation-limited tool contract, an ambiguous timeout after a non-idempotent external action cannot be resolved reliably by local checkpointing, replanning, or retry alone. If the action either committed or did not commit, those histories are indistinguishable to recovery, and repeated calls create additional effects, no recovery policy guarantees exactly one effect in both histories. Its worst-case success probability is at most 1/2. This is a conditional impossibility result, not an empirical estimate of agent reliability.
output.method: Construct two minimal execution histories with identical agent-visible transcripts but different external states, then couple the recovery policy's randomness to prove an upper bound. The hypothesis is that recovery requires information about external commitment or a stronger execution contract, not merely better reasoning over the same transcript. The competing claim—that local rollback plus retry suffices—is separated by a committed action whose acknowledgment is lost. A proposed paired fault-injection test would compare stopping, checkpoint-and-retry, restarting, and replay through an atomic deduplication interface against an evaluator-only effect ledger. No runtime or external-source retrieval is available; the derivation below is analytical and the implementation test is unexecuted.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the task, tool contract, and success event
reasoning_steps.argument: The task is to create exactly one irreversible external effect, represented by an integer counter N initially equal to zero. Each executed call to apply(payload) increments N by one; acknowledgments do not reveal N. There is no decrement, cancellation, status query, deduplication, or other observation of N available to the agent. Evaluation occurs at a fixed finite horizon T after recovery terminates. Effect-level success is N=1; truthful completion and safe handling of uncertainty are additional metrics, not substitutes for this condition. Any stronger end-to-end success requirement implies effect-level success, so an upper bound on the latter also bounds the former.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct the indistinguishable failure pair
reasoning_steps.argument: In history H0, the initial request is discarded without execution and the client receives a timeout, leaving N=0. In history H1, the initial request executes, its acknowledgment is lost, and the client receives the same timeout, leaving N=1. The local checkpoint, request bytes, timing observations, and all other agent-visible information are identical. The initial request is quiescent in both histories: it cannot execute later. Every subsequent recovery call, if any, executes once and receives the same generic acknowledgment on the same schedule in both histories. These are two admissible schedules under the stated contract, not claims about their prevalence.

reasoning_steps.title: Adaptive reasoning cannot distinguish these histories
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix the recovery policy's internal random choices, including stochastic model decisions. Initially its observable state is identical in H0 and H1. If its observed histories remain identical through one step, its next action is identical; a wait, local operation, or repeated call then receives an identical observation by construction. Induction therefore gives identical recovery transcripts and the same number R of additional calls. Removing the conditioning on randomness shows that R has the same distribution in both histories. Checkpoint restoration and a fresh agent run do not invalidate this argument if they have only the specified observations and actions.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive the impossibility and tight minimax bound
reasoning_steps.argument: At the horizon, H0 has N=R and H1 has N=1+R. Success in H0 therefore requires R=1, while success in H1 requires R=0. Consequently s0=Pr(R=1) and s1=Pr(R=0), with s0+s1<=1 and min(s0,s1)<=1/2. The effect-level bound is tight: a policy that makes exactly one additional call with probability 1/2 and otherwise makes none achieves success probability 1/2 in each history. Deterministic stopping yields counts (0,1), one retry yields (1,2), and two or more retries fail in both. If the committed history has a known prior probability p, optimal average effect-level success is max(p,1-p); that prior does not provide a guarantee for each history. Abstention can avoid a false completion claim but cannot guarantee task completion.

reasoning_steps.title: Locate the failure propagation and recovery boundary
reasoning_steps.argument: The initiating fault is loss of information about external commitment, not necessarily an incorrect plan or model judgment. It creates uncertainty between N=0 and N=1. Blind retry converts that uncertainty into a duplicate effect in H1; refusing to retry leaves an omission in H0. Restoring local memory does not restore external state. A more capable model or another critic given the same information cannot eliminate this ambiguity. This does not refute recovery in systems with additional observations, reversible effects, or stronger tool contracts; those systems fall outside the construction.

reasoning_steps.title: State a sufficient changed contract rather than a universal remedy
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider instead a tool that accepts a logical-operation key k and immutable payload, atomically couples its effect with a durable record for k, and returns the stored result on every replay. The client durably records k before the first dispatch and reuses it across restarts; the service retains its record throughout the retry horizon. With no other writers, atomic deduplication makes the number of effects for k at most one. If at least one invocation is processed successfully by T, it is also at least one, so N=1. This is a conditional safety-and-completion argument: deduplication alone does not guarantee availability or delivery. Merely attaching a request ID does not establish the contract; an effect followed by a crash before a separate deduplication write still permits duplication.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify a discriminating implementation test and independent oracle
reasoning_steps.argument: Build a controlled append-only effect service with an evaluator-only durable ledger. Inject either discard-before-execution or commit-then-drop-ack, exposing byte-identical timeout transcripts and matched timing to the agent. Test policies that stop, restore-and-retry, restart-and-retry, or replay a persisted key through the atomic service. For deterministic one-retry policies, the predicted baseline effect counts are respectively (0,1), (1,2), and (1,2) across the two faults. Keyed replay predicts (1,1), provided replay processing occurs before the deadline. Also inject a crash between effect creation and a non-atomic deduplication write; duplication would distinguish a genuine atomic contract from a merely labeled idempotency mechanism. The oracle checks actual ledger entries, not the agent's summary. Record false completion, unresolved termination, extra effects, calls, and latency separately. Keep model and prompt versions, task, permissions, deadline, and retry budget fixed; report keyed-service overhead rather than treating it as free. First verify the deterministic service behavior without a model, then use paired seeds to study whether agents actually follow the recovery protocol.

reasoning_steps.title: Assess contribution and scope
reasoning_steps.argument: The contribution is a concrete failure-chain specimen and an exact limit on information-limited recovery, useful for selecting fault-injection cases and rejecting overbroad claims about local checkpointing. It uses a standard indistinguishability argument, not a demonstrated novel recovery architecture. No domain literature, deployed implementation, or agent benchmark has been inspected here, so novelty relative to established work and empirical generality are not assessed. The proposed test evaluates a narrow tool contract; it would not establish overall reliability on long, open-ended tasks.

assumptions: The task requires exactly one irreversible external effect; every executed repeated call adds another effect, and no compensating operation is available.
Both initial histories are admissible, have identical agent-visible observations, and have no outstanding initial request that can execute later.
Recovery can only wait, perform local operations, stop, or repeat the action; it cannot inspect external commitment through another channel.
Subsequent calls execute once and return indistinguishable generic acknowledgments in the two histories.
Recovery is evaluated within a finite horizon, and policy randomness has the same distribution in both histories.
output.evidence_status: A conditional analytical counterexample and probability bound are derived above; they have not been formally verified. No computation, implementation experiment, literature inspection, or empirical agent-reliability result is claimed.
open_obligations: Implement the paired fault histories and verify that the agent-visible transcripts, including timing and metadata, are indistinguishable while the evaluator ledger differs.
Test whether an actual tool's deduplication contract atomically covers the external effect, survives crashes, retains records long enough, and preserves keys across agent restarts.
Execute the controlled policy comparison and measure false completion, duplicate effects, unresolved outcomes, latency, and cost; predicted outcomes are not measurements.

Extend the analysis to delayed initial requests, concurrent writers, partial multi-resource effects, and authorized compensations; the present proof does not establish recovery guarantees for those domains.
Inspect relevant distributed-systems literature and documented agent recovery designs before making novelty or prevalence claims.

output.response:
Cycle 1 establishes a useful conditional measurement result, not an empirical agent-reliability finding. The acceptance/correctness decomposition, explicit ranking reversal, and simultaneous finite-cohort audit certificate are mathematically convincing under the stated sampling and oracle assumptions. Neither independence among agent runs nor independence among audit cells is needed.

The strongest unresolved premise is reference-label accuracy. An independent sensitivity check makes its importance precise: if an audit bounds the cohort prevalence of reference labels Z by [L,U], and an externally justified bound gives Pr(Y != Z) <= delta over that same cohort, then true correctness lies in [max(0,L-delta), min(1,U+delta)] on the audit coverage event. Without any restriction connecting Z to Y, even a complete audit of Z can leave true correctness anywhere in [0,1]. Thus more precise auditing cannot repair an unvalidated oracle.

No benchmark, scoring implementation, external-state record, or execution was supplied. Both runtimes are unavailable. The proposed framework therefore remains analytical; practical usefulness, novelty, deployment generality, and intervention benefits are unassessed. The next useful step is a sharp sensitivity certificate that exposes rather than assumes away reference-oracle error.
objections: Material, recoverable evidence gap: the accurate-reference premise is unvalidated. Shared evaluator blind spots can survive exhaustive auditing and invalidate interpretation as external correctness.
Material scope limitation: finite-cohort label recovery does not establish deployment reliability, causal intervention benefit, recovery quality, or resource efficiency.
The cycle-1 ranking reversal decisively refutes identification of correctness ranking from acceptance labels alone; it does not refute the proposed audit protocol or the broader project.
remaining_obligations: o1: Inspect an actual benchmark's scoring implementation, task manifest, horizon, and authoritative external-state records.
o2: Validate or explicitly bound reference-oracle errors.

NOT_FOUND means that the initial request has not committed at the query's linearization point, not that it cannot commit later. A discarded request and a pending request can therefore require incompatible recovery actions. A sufficient stronger contract is durable cancellation serialized with the actual external effect: it must either certify the existing commitment or permanently prevent that request from committing. This provides at-most-one safety; exactly-one completion additionally requires successful processing and, for confirmed completion, delivery of the relevant responses.
output.method: Analytical schedule construction and state-machine invariant proof; no experiment is executed or requested. The hypothesis is that observing absence of commitment is weaker than establishing final nonexecution. The competing claim predicts that retry after a linearizable NOT_FOUND is safe; an explicit schedule in which the old request commits after the replacement discriminates against it. reasoning_steps.title: Define the execution and observation contract
reasoning_steps.argument: Let N initially be zero. Executing the initial request r or a replacement r' creates one irreversible effect and increments N. Each individual dispatched request executes at most once, but different requests are not deduplicated against one another. There are no other effect-producing writers or compensations. A client timeout need not terminate r. Give the proposed status interface its strongest relevant read semantics: status(r) is linearizable with r's actual effect commitment, returns COMMITTED with a durable result if that commitment precedes its linearization point, and otherwise returns NOT_FOUND. It does not report pending execution or inhibit future commitment. The commitment record has no visibility gap or expiration during the analysis. Thus the counterexample does not depend on stale reads or non-atomic recording.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct the discarded schedule
reasoning_steps.argument: Choose ordered events t0<t1<t2<t3<t4<t5<T. At t0 the client dispatches r. In schedule D, r is permanently discarded without execution. At t1 the client observes a timeout. At t2 status(r) linearizes and at t3 returns NOT_FOUND. At t4 recovery dispatches r'; at t5 r' executes and is acknowledged. N(T)=1. No observation of the initial timeout or NOT_FOUND proves that this discarded schedule, rather than a delayed schedule, occurred.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct the pending schedule with the same recovery prefix
reasoning_steps.argument: In schedule P, r is retained but not executed through t5. The timeout, query invocation, NOT_FOUND reply, replacement execution, acknowledgment, timing, and metadata through t5 match D. The query is legal: r had not committed at t2. At a further event t6 with t5<t6<T, r executes, and its acknowledgment is lost. Hence N(T)=2. An independent check is the legal linearization order status(r) < commit(r') < commit(r): the read and both effects satisfy their specifications. There is no contradiction with linearizability.

reasoning_steps.title: Establish the safety-versus-completion obstruction beyond one retry policy
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider any finite recovery prefix ending in its first replacement dispatch on a discarded execution. Before that dispatch, a pending execution can have exactly the same observations: postpone r's commitment past every completed status query and every wait in the prefix. The replacement can then commit, followed by r, producing two effects. Thus any policy that permits such a replacement prefix cannot guarantee at-most-one safety for all admissible schedules. Conversely, never replacing r cannot achieve exactly-one completion in D. Repeated queries and finite waiting merely lengthen the indistinguishable prefix. A randomized policy cannot give a zero-error guarantee by assigning positive probability to an unsafe replacement decision; this argument asserts no numerical minimax bound for the changed model. Waiting indefinitely avoids this particular duplicate but abandons completion in D.

reasoning_steps.title: Identify the precise propagation mechanism and scope change
reasoning_steps.argument: The failure chain is timeout → accurate observation of current noncommitment → unjustified inference of final nonexecution → replacement → delayed original commitment → duplicate effect. This is a check-then-act race, not a stale-query fault or necessarily a reasoning-capability deficit. A post-retry query may detect the duplicate but cannot undo an irreversible effect. The prior artifact excluded pending initial requests and status queries, so its count equations and 1/2 bound are not premises here. Its narrow conclusion about local state not restoring external state remains compatible with this new construction. A status operation that also closes execution is outside the read-only contract and is precisely the stronger mechanism considered next.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify a sufficient durable cancellation contract
reasoning_steps.argument: Associate r and its immutable payload with durable state S_r in {OPEN, COMMITTED(result), CANCELLED}, initially logically OPEN even if the request has not arrived. All effect attempts and seal(r) operations serialize on this state. commit(r) may create its effect only by an atomic transition OPEN → COMMITTED(result) that includes the actual irreversible effect. If S_r is CANCELLED or COMMITTED, it creates no further effect. seal(r) atomically changes OPEN → CANCELLED and returns CANCELLED, or returns the existing COMMITTED result or CANCELLED state without changing it. A cancellation tombstone must be created even when r is absent from the server, survive crashes, and remain effective for every possible delayed arrival or worker. Repeating seal after a lost reply is safe. Neither terminal state expires while an old request can still execute.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive the recovery protocol and its race outcomes
reasoning_steps.argument: After the timeout, invoke seal(r); do not dispatch a replacement until its terminal outcome is known. If it returns COMMITTED, accept that result and issue no replacement. If it returns CANCELLED, dispatch at most one replacement r', using the base model's guarantee that this subsequent invocation executes once and returns its acknowledgment. There are only two possible race orders from OPEN. If commit(r) wins, N becomes one and every seal returns COMMITTED. If seal(r) wins, r is permanently unable to increment N and a replacement is permitted. A timeout of seal is not a CANCELLED result: recovery repeats seal or remains unresolved rather than speculating.

reasoning_steps.title: Prove at-most-one safety independently of progress
reasoning_steps.argument: Before recovery, r contributes at most one effect. After a COMMITTED seal outcome, the protocol issues no replacement and r's terminal state prevents further effects. After a CANCELLED seal outcome, r contributes zero effects for the entire execution: it could not have committed before that outcome, since COMMITTED is terminal, and cannot commit afterward. The controller then issues at most one replacement, which contributes at most one effect. These cases imply N≤1 at every time, including after recovery terminates and after any evaluation deadline. Communication loss may block progress but cannot violate this invariant if an unknown seal outcome never authorizes a replacement. This proves safety for arbitrary ordering of r and seal under the specified contract.

reasoning_steps.title: Prove conditional completion and distinguish knowledge from effects
reasoning_steps.argument: Suppose repeated seal invocations eventually receive a terminal response. A COMMITTED response already certifies N=1. A CANCELLED response leaves N=0, and successful processing of the single replacement makes N=1; its acknowledgment permits confirmed completion. Thus eventual confirmed completion requires both eventual resolution of seal and, on the cancelled branch, successful replacement processing and response delivery. No finite deadline follows merely from linearizability or cancellation. For completion by T, those branch-specific events must occur by T; known latency bounds could establish this, whereas fairness alone cannot. If a replacement acknowledgment can also be lost, the base model's reliable-subsequent-call premise no longer holds: unresolved recovery recurs for r', and this single-replacement protocol does not establish confirmed completion in that enlarged domain.

reasoning_steps.argument: Cancellation that only removes queued work is insufficient if an already-running worker can still commit. Likewise, checking a fencing token before a network call is insufficient: a worker can pass the check, pause, be fenced out, and later complete the irreversible effect downstream. The required exclusion must hold at the actual effect boundary, or a cancellation barrier must wait for all earlier authorized work to settle and report COMMITTED if any committed. A cancellation ACK meaning only 'request received' does not certify CANCELLED. These distinctions explain why the state machine is a sufficient specification, not evidence that an ordinary cancellation endpoint implements it.

If m_c records were audited and k_c had Z=1, the observed labels also imply k_c<=T_c<=n_c-m_c+k_c. Consequently define J_c^- = max(k_c,ceil(n_c l_c)) and J_c^+ = min(n_c-m_c+k_c,floor(n_c u_c)). On the simultaneous coverage event, T_c is an integer in [J_c^-,J_c^+]. Exhaustive auditing gives J_c^-=J_c^+=k_c. For an unaudited cell use m_c=k_c=0 and [l_c,u_c]=[0,1]. An empty feasible interval indicates incompatible constraints; it must not be reported as a correctness certificate.

reasoning_steps.title: A reproducible way to obtain the audit coverage premise
reasoning_steps.argument: One conservative construction reuses the finite-population sampling design in the supplied prior extract. For K nonempty cells, prespecify positive sample sizes and sample uniformly without replacement. In a nonexhaustive sampled cell set zhat_c=k_c/m_c, t_c=sqrt(log(2K/alpha)/(2m_c)), and [l_c,u_c]=[max(0,zhat_c-t_c),min(1,zhat_c+t_c)]. The standard without-replacement Hoeffding inequality gives cell failure probability at most 2 exp(-2m_c t_c^2)=alpha/K. Use exact reference prevalence for exhaustive cells and [0,1] for unsampled cells. A union bound establishes simultaneous coverage at least 1-alpha, without independence across cells or agent executions. The result below also accepts other valid simultaneous intervals; it does not claim these conservative intervals are statistically optimal.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive sharp cellwise true-correctness bounds
reasoning_steps.argument: For fixed T_c=t, changing at most D_c binary labels gives max(0,t-D_c)<=S_c<=min(n_c,t+D_c), since each disagreement changes the positive count by at most one. The lower endpoint is attained by changing min(t,D_c) reference-positive labels to zero; the upper endpoint by changing min(n_c-t,D_c) reference-negative labels to one. Optimizing over the feasible reference counts therefore gives B_c^- = max(0,J_c^- - D_c) and B_c^+ = min(n_c,J_c^+ + D_c). These endpoints are attainable: choose a reference vector matching the observed sample and the selected feasible endpoint count, then perform the indicated flips. Every integer between the endpoints is also attainable, because the fixed-t integer intervals overlap or are adjacent as t advances by one. Thus this is an exact projection of the stated cell information, not just a triangle-inequality outer bound.

reasoning_steps.title: Aggregate correctness and differences, with a precise sharpness qualification
reasoning_steps.argument: Set L_a=(sum_{c belonging to a} B_c^-)/N_a and U_a=(sum_{c belonging to a} B_c^+)/N_a. On the simultaneous audit event, p_a=sum_i Y_ai/N_a lies in [L_a,U_a], and p_A-p_B lies in [L_A-U_B,U_A-L_B]. With no additional cross-cell or cross-agent constraints, all lower cell endpoints can be attained together, as can all upper endpoints; choosing A lower and B upper attains the lower difference endpoint, and reversing choices attains the upper. These are therefore sharp interval hulls relative to the supplied rectangular audit bounds, sample observations, and disagreement budgets. A joint audit region or substantive coupling between records could narrow them. A strict A advantage is certified precisely when L_A>U_B; equality permits a tie.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate the simple rate formula from the exact finite-count result
reasoning_steps.argument: Ignoring integer rounding and sample-support tightening, the cell rate bounds are max(0,l_c-delta_c) and min(1,u_c+delta_c). Weighting these by n_c/N_a gives a convenient conservative correctness interval. The exact finite-count formulas above can be narrower. Sharpness here concerns compatible labels given the audit region; it does not mean the audit confidence procedure has minimum width. If delta_c=0, the result reduces to the reference-prevalence certificate. If delta_c=1 in every cell, the result becomes [0,1] for each agent regardless of audit precision.

reasoning_steps.title: Apply the certificate to reference scores of 90 versus 80
reasoning_steps.argument: Use the supplied construction with 100 records per agent, 90 accepted for A and 80 for B, and suppose a complete reference audit gives Z=O. Then A has reference-positive counts (90,0) and B has (80,0) in their accepted/rejected cells. The exact difference interval is [(10-D_A+-D_B-)/100,(10+D_A-+D_B+)/100], where D_A+=floor(90 delta_A+), D_A-=floor(10 delta_A-), D_B+=floor(80 delta_B+), and D_B-=floor(20 delta_B-). Thus A's strict advantage survives exactly when D_A+ + D_B- < 10. Only errors that lower A's accepted-cell correctness or raise B's rejected-cell correctness threaten this certificate; the other two budgets affect its upper endpoint. The rate relaxation certifies A when 0.9 delta_A+ + 0.2 delta_B- < 0.1.

reasoning_steps.title: Check the common-bound threshold and its boundary counterexample exactly
reasoning_steps.argument: If all four cells share the same bound delta=d, the rate relaxation requires d<1/11. The exact 100-record certificate instead holds for every d<0.10: then floor(90d)<=8 and floor(20d)<=1, so the lower difference is at least 1/100. At d=0.10, the allowed counts are 9 and 2, producing lower difference -1/100. This endpoint is attained by flipping nine A accepted references from correct to incorrect and two B rejected references from incorrect to correct, giving true correctness 81% versus 82%. Thus the finite-cohort common-bound threshold is exactly d<0.10, not d<1/11. This difference is an integer-budget effect, not additional evidence about oracle quality. As a check, d=0.05 gives the exact interval [0.05,0.14], from budgets (D_A+,D_A-,D_B+,D_B-)=(4,0,4,1).

reasoning_steps.title: Check the alternative reference audit rather than identifying acceptance with correctness
reasoning_steps.argument: In the second configuration of the supplied example, a full reference audit could instead show 70 reference-positive records in A's accepted cell, zero in A's rejected cell, and B reference counts (80,0). Then U_A=[min(90,70+D_A+)+D_A-]/100 and L_B=(80-D_B+)/100. B's strict advantage is certified exactly when D_B+ + D_A+ + D_A- < 10. To see necessity despite the clipping, if D_A+>=20 then U_A>=0.90>L_B; otherwise the clipping is inactive and the inequality follows directly. Acceptance remains 90 versus 80 in both configurations. The audit distinguishes their Z distributions, but only justified disagreement budgets transfer that distinction into a Y ranking.

reasoning_steps.title: Show what exhaustive auditing cannot identify
reasoning_steps.argument: Without any justified constraint linking Z to Y, hold every observed O, every audited Z, and all nondiagnostic logs fixed. Assign Y=0 to all records or Y=1 to all records; both assignments remain compatible with these observations. More generally every finite-cohort correctness count from 0 through N_a is possible. Across agents, choosing opposite assignments attains differences -1 and +1. Hence the correctness interval hull is [0,1] per agent and the difference interval hull is [-1,1]; neither ranking, false-acceptance rate, nor false-rejection rate is identified. This claim excludes observations that themselves determine Y. More reference audits or agreement among critics with shared blind spots cannot establish a disagreement bound by themselves.

reasoning_steps.title: Keep oracle validation, peer evidence, and deployment inference separate
reasoning_steps.argument: If the delta bounds are themselves simultaneous confidence bounds with failure probability beta, combine that validation event with the reference-audit event to obtain coverage at least 1-alpha-beta by a union bound; no independence is required. This requires actual valid validation evidence for the same target cells, not a guessed delta. The bounded peer extract 29362c57-cbcb-4127-8b3d-3976a3e3e206 discusses hidden external commitment under ambiguous tool timeouts. Its assumptions differ from this measurement model and its source is incomplete, so its probability bound is not transferred. Its warning motivates checking authoritative external state, but does not validate an oracle here. The present result addresses the sensitivity component of o2/o12, while leaving their empirical premise unresolved; o1/o3/o4/o5 and their duplicate ledger entries remain open. Novelty, practical benefit, and deployment generality have not been assessed.

output.claim: Conditional on authoritative validation labels, fixed finite cohorts, prespecified uniform sampling without replacement, and cohort-wide knowledge that Z=O, a 95% simultaneous cellwise certificate can establish A's strict correctness advantage after zero observed disagreements using 43 validation labels: 23 from A's 90 accepted records and all 20 of B's rejected records. This is the minimum within the specified hypergeometric cellwise-bound procedure with freely prespecified error-budget allocation and union-bound composition. It is not a minimum over all possible joint inference procedures. The validation is designed, not executed.
output.method: Derive exact finite-population disagreement bounds by inverting the probability of observing zero disagreements, prove simultaneous coverage without independence, and optimize the validation design analytically. The discriminating outcome is whether the resulting worst-case correctness difference is positive; reference agreement alone does not distinguish genuinely correct outputs from shared oracle blind spots. The numerical design assumes Z=O is established throughout the relevant cohort by complete reference inspection, so reference-audit error spending is zero. With sampled reference auditing, its error budget must also be included. Review the supplied prior and peer extracts as unverified inputs, retaining the acceptance-only counterexample as a negative constraint. Neither runtime nor external-source retrieval is available; no validation, benchmark, or computational search was executed.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the population, labels, and ranking-threatening cells
reasoning_steps.argument: There are 100 fixed records per agent. A has 90 accepted and 10 rejected records; B has 80 accepted and 20 rejected records. O is evaluator acceptance, Z is the fixed reference label, and Y is binary external correctness under the frozen rubric and horizon H. Let d_c be the actual whole-cell number of Z/Y disagreements. When Z=O throughout the cohort, A has at least 90-d_A+ correct records and B has at most 80+d_B- correct records. Therefore p_A-p_B >= (10-d_A+-d_B-)/100. Errors in A's rejected cell or B's accepted cell cannot worsen this lower bound. They need not be validated for this one-sided claim.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify an independently grounded validation stage
reasoning_steps.argument: Before drawing samples, freeze record identities, cell membership, Z labels, model/prompt/tool versions, budgets, rubric, and H. Prespecify sample sizes and randomization; sample uniformly without replacement from every targeted whole cell, not merely from previously convenient audit records. Validation obtains Y from external state and constraint-relevant event history, not from completion text or a second model's agreement. A concrete admissible domain is a closed transactional sandbox whose actual-effect ledger and immutable terminal snapshot completely determine the rubric. Its declared execution window must leave enough time for bounded drain or effect fencing, terminal inspection, and adjudication by H. The validator is operationally separate from the agent and reference evaluator, and blinded to agent identity where feasible. Sampling or validation must not alter the original outcome. These are proposed requirements, not demonstrated capabilities of a supplied system.

reasoning_steps.title: State precisely what makes a validation label authoritative
reasoning_steps.argument: Authority requires a justified correspondence between the observed records and every rubric-relevant actual effect: correct record identity and timestamps, complete observation of all relevant writers and side effects, accurate durable history, correct postcondition checks, and enough history to detect intermediate constraint violations as well as terminal failure. A terminal snapshot alone is insufficient when earlier forbidden effects matter. All selected records must be ascertainable; unavailable evidence cannot be silently excluded or labeled as agreement. A replay ordinarily labels a new execution, not the original one. In the proposed bounded sandbox, terminated or fenced writers make the inspected terminal state stable through H. An unbounded asynchronous service without such a contract does not satisfy this premise merely because a status query says NOT_FOUND. Outcomes beyond the declared rubric/horizon remain outside the claim.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive the zero-disagreement sampling probability
reasoning_steps.argument: In a fixed cell of size n containing d disagreements, a size-m uniform sample has X disagreements. Exactly C(n-d,m) of the C(n,m) possible samples contain none. Thus h(n,m,d)=P_d(X=0)=C(n-d,m)/C(n,m)=C(n-m,d)/C(n,d), taking a binomial coefficient as zero when its lower argument exceeds its upper argument. This is a whole-population statement under random sampling; it requires no independent errors or independent agent executions. For fixed n,m, h is nonincreasing in d. The two expressions independently count the same event by selecting agreement records or placing all disagreements outside the sample.

reasoning_steps.title: Invert the probability into a valid count bound
reasoning_steps.argument: Prespecify a cell error allowance beta with 0<beta<1. On observing X=0, define U(n,m;beta)=max{d in {0,...,n}: h(n,m,d)>beta}; on X>0, return the conservative bound n. For a fixed true d, undercoverage can occur only when X=0 and d>U. Monotonicity then gives P_d(undercoverage)=h(n,m,d)<=beta. Consequently d<=U has unconditional coverage at least 1-beta. This confidence statement is not a posterior probability conditional on observing zero. At m=0 the bound is n. A census reveals d exactly; for a zero-disagreement census use U=0 with failure allowance zero. For nonzero observations, a prespecified full hypergeometric inversion could replace the deliberately conservative fallback.

reasoning_steps.title: Obtain simultaneous coverage and compose with reference auditing
reasoning_steps.argument: For prespecified validation allowances beta_c, the union bound gives P(all d_c<=U_c)>=1-sum_c beta_c. No independence between cells, validation labels, or agent runs is required. Let the reference audit simultaneously cover every cell's reference-positive count T_c by [J_c^-,J_c^+] with failure probability at most alpha. On the intersection event, each true-positive count lies between max(0,J_c^- - U_c) and min(n_c,J_c^+ + U_c). Aggregating those endpoints gives correctness and difference bounds with coverage at least 1-alpha-sum_c beta_c. Overlap or dependence between reference auditing and validation is allowed provided each procedure retains its claimed marginal coverage. Outcome-driven changes to sample sizes or error allocations are not justified by this fixed-design argument.

reasoning_steps.title: Make the optimization criterion explicit
reasoning_steps.argument: For the numerical design, complete reference inspection establishes Z=O, hence alpha=0. A positive lower difference requires U_A+ + U_B- <=9. Write their proposed upper limits as a and b with a+b=9; using smaller sums cannot improve feasibility. To achieve these limits after zero observations, it suffices and, for these inverted bounds, is necessary that h(90,m_A,a+1)<=beta_A and h(20,m_B,b+1)<=beta_B. With freely prespecified nonnegative allowances totaling at most 1/20, the feasibility criterion is therefore h(90,m_A,10-b)+h(20,m_B,b+1)<=1/20 for some integer b=0,...,9. Zero allowance here is used for an exact census. This specifies the procedure class in which the minimum is claimed.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct the 43-label certificate
reasoning_steps.argument: Prespecify m_A=23, m_B=20, beta_A=1/20 and beta_B=0. B's zero-disagreement census establishes d_B-=0 exactly. For A, h(90,23,10)=C(67,10)/C(90,10)<1/20, while h(90,23,9)=C(67,9)/C(90,9)>1/20. Thus the inverted upper bound is U_A+=9. On the 95% coverage event, p_A>=81/100 and p_B<=80/100, so p_A-p_B>=1/100. This certifies a strict finite-cohort advantage, not equivalence to a 90% versus 80% true-correctness comparison.

reasoning_steps.title: Exclude totals of 42 or fewer: boundary and low-b cases
reasoning_steps.argument: Because h decreases with sample size, it suffices to exclude total 42; any smaller design can be augmented to 42. Put t=m_B and m_A=42-t. For b=0, B's probability is (20-t)/20, forcing t>=19. At t=19 it already consumes 1/20 and A's probability is positive; at t=20, A's probability is C(68,10)/C(90,10)>1/20. For b=1, requiring each probability individually to be at most 1/20 forces 16<=t<=17: B excludes t<=15, while A excludes t>=18 since C(66,9)/C(90,9)>1/20. Throughout this remaining range their sum is at least C(64,9)/C(90,9)+3/190>1/20. For b=2 the analogous necessary range is 12<=t<=14. Throughout it the sum is at least C(60,8)/C(90,8)+20/1140>1/20. These are exact rational comparisons, obtained by cross multiplication.

reasoning_steps.title: Complete the minimum proof
reasoning_steps.argument: For b=3, individual probability constraints force 10<=t<=11. Throughout that range the sum is at least C(58,7)/C(90,7)+126/4845>1/20. For b=4, the individual constraints require m_A>=35 and m_B>=9, already totaling at least 44: C(56,6)/C(90,6)>1/20 and C(12,5)/C(20,5)>1/20 establish the necessary thresholds. For b=5 they require m_A>=40 and m_B>=7, totaling at least 47: use C(51,5)/C(90,5)>1/20 and C(14,6)/C(20,6)>1/20. For b>=6, A's tested count 10-b is at most four, and even m_A=42 gives h>=C(48,4)/C(90,4)>1/20. All b are excluded at total 42. Together with the construction, this proves the minimum 43 within the declared procedure class.

reasoning_steps.title: Explain error-budget and method sensitivity
reasoning_steps.argument: The minimum uses asymmetric allocation: an exact census of the small threatening cell and all statistical error allowance in the larger cell. It must not be reported as a result for a fixed equal-tail design. If both cells are assigned beta=0.025 in advance, a feasible design is m_A=32,m_B=14, with upper counts eight and one respectively; that is a different design. If reference auditing spends alpha>0, validation has only 0.05-alpha available, and feasibility must be recomputed using that smaller budget. The 43-label construction remains valid only when alpha+C(67,10)/C(90,10)<=0.05. A nonrectangular joint confidence region or an additional independence assumption could change the optimum; no global sample-complexity optimality is asserted.

reasoning_steps.argument: I examined the supplied bounded source extract 496ed077-19aa-4a3d-a216-0a51cf23c866 and target extract e9b2a9ae-e383-4499-8431-4c4ef4b7e5f7. output.claim: Conditional on the asynchronous, nonparticipating downstream contract specified below, no wrapper can guarantee both sound CANCELLED authorization for replacement and eventual conclusive recovery resolution. Durable wrapper records and upstream fencing cannot exclude an already-dispatched downstream effect. A finite cancellation decision in a discarded execution has an indistinguishable delayed execution in which the original still commits. The result changes only when recovery can obtain authoritative evidence distinguishing permanent nonexecution from possible later execution, together with the progress conditions needed to obtain that evidence.
output.method: Analytical indistinguishability construction and case analysis; no computation or implementation experiment. Hypothesis: local durability and fencing cannot manufacture exclusion at a nonparticipating irreversible-effect boundary. The competing claim predicts that revoking the local token and recording cancellation suffice after timeout; the discriminating schedule releases an already-dispatched downstream call after that cancellation. Define resolution as a truthful COMMITTED outcome or sound CANCELLED authorization, not merely returning UNKNOWN. Give the wrapper reliable local storage, continued execution, and even accurate read-only commitment queries; the obstruction therefore does not depend on wrapper crashes, stale reads, or unavailable local infrastructure. Examine the supplied cycle-2 extract and peer handoff as unverified research inputs, independently derive the schedules, and specify sufficient changed contracts without assuming their implementability.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the effect, authorization, and progress contracts
reasoning_steps.argument: Let E_r(t) be the number of actual irreversible effects of the original request r by time t, initially zero and restricted to {0,1}. A distinct replacement r' can independently add one effect, with no cross-request deduplication or compensation. Sound CANCELLED at time t means that r has produced no effect and cannot produce one in any admissible continuation after authorization. COMMITTED must certify an actual effect, not merely a wrapper record or dispatch. Conclusive-resolution liveness requires an eventual known COMMITTED or sound CANCELLED outcome on every admissible execution. Exactly-one task completion further requires that any authorized replacement execute and, for confirmed completion, that its outcome become known.

reasoning_steps.title: Isolate the uncontrolled downstream boundary
reasoning_steps.argument: The wrapper can durably record r, prevent new wrapper dispatches, increment fencing epochs, and reject stale local workers. But r has already crossed that boundary: downstream may discard it permanently or retain it for an arbitrarily long finite delay before executing. The downstream effect neither consults the wrapper's current token nor serializes with its record updates. No available observation certifies permanent downstream nonexecution. If read-only commitment queries exist, grant them accurate linearizable answers: an uncommitted pending request and a discarded request both yield absence. These premises are stronger for the wrapper than unreliable local storage, but still permit the required paired histories.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct the discarded execution
reasoning_steps.argument: In execution D, the wrapper durably records r with token e, dispatches it, and receives a timeout after downstream discards r without effect. The wrapper continues running and all its local operations finish. Every commitment query reports absence. Thus E_r remains zero forever. A truthful COMMITTED result is impossible in D. If conclusive-resolution liveness holds, the wrapper must eventually return CANCELLED at some finite event τ. Its entire visible prefix through τ includes records, token values, query replies, clocks, timing, and any locally generated cancellation acknowledgment.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct an indistinguishable delayed execution
reasoning_steps.argument: In execution P, downstream retains the dispatched r but performs no effect through τ. Schedule the same wrapper steps, clock observations, query replies, and local responses as in D. Inductively, identical visible input and identical policy choices yield identical wrapper state and outputs: record writes and fencing increments therefore also match. The absence queries are legal because r has not committed. The wrapper consequently returns the same CANCELLED authorization at τ. After τ, downstream executes r without consulting the now-revoked token. This is an allowed continuation of P and contradicts the authorization's permanent-nonexecution meaning.

reasoning_steps.title: Check the user-visible consequence independently
reasoning_steps.argument: Suppose the authorized replacement executes once and is acknowledged between τ and the delayed original's execution. In D the final total E_r + E_r' is 0 + 1 = 1. In P it is 1 + 1 = 2. The event order dispatch(r) < timeout < local revoke < CANCELLED < effect(r') < effect(r) is consistent with every stated interface: none constrains the final downstream effect by the local revoke. This explicit legal ordering independently checks the indistinguishability argument. Even without replacement, the late effect already falsifies CANCELLED; replacement converts that false certificate into a duplicate irreversible action.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate safety, liveness, and administrative termination
reasoning_steps.argument: Therefore no universally sound wrapper can return CANCELLED at any finite prefix of D: each such prefix has a delayed continuation like P. It also cannot truthfully return COMMITTED in D. Waiting preserves safety but violates conclusive-resolution liveness there. Returning UNKNOWN, escalating, or stopping can be safe administrative termination, but is not authorization for replacement and does not satisfy the defined resolution guarantee. A finite evaluation deadline does not eliminate the hazard: r can execute after that deadline. The argument covers deterministic policies and guarantees required for every fixed random tape; no numerical probability bound or almost-sure termination theorem is claimed.

reasoning_steps.title: Identify the logically necessary information
reasoning_steps.argument: Let Compatible(h) be the executions consistent with a visible history h at authorization. A necessary condition for sound CANCELLED is that every execution in Compatible(h), under every allowed continuation, has zero original effects. Hence a useful cancellation certificate must establish both no prior effect and exclusion of every future original effect. Local revocation establishes only that no new compliant wrapper dispatch is allowed; it does not satisfy either external-state claim for the outstanding call. To restore conclusive resolution in discarded executions, some such distinguishing certificate must also eventually become obtainable. This is a semantic requirement, not a claim that there is one uniquely weakest API.

reasoning_steps.title: Give a sufficient downstream-participation contract
reasoning_steps.argument: One sufficient changed contract is the cycle-2 seal specification: the actual effect and durable per-request state transition serialize, with terminal COMMITTED and CANCELLED states. Seal must return COMMITTED if the effect won, or durably prevent every later effect attempt if cancellation won, including delayed arrivals and already-authorized work. If COMMITTED wins, issue no replacement and the total is one. If CANCELLED wins, the original contributes zero forever, so at most one single-execution replacement preserves total ≤ 1. Eventual delivery of a terminal seal result gives conclusive original-request resolution; replacement processing and acknowledgment are additional premises for confirmed task completion. A token check followed by an independently scheduled effect is insufficient because cancellation can occur between them. This is a sufficient specification only, not an implementation established for the stipulated downstream tool.

reasoning_steps.title: Give an alternative certified-quiescence contract
reasoning_steps.argument: Atomic effect-record coupling is not logically necessary if a different authoritative mechanism closes the uncertainty. Suppose a certificate at barrier b proves that no old downstream attempt can produce an effect after b, and the wrapper has durably closed all new dispatch paths for r. Then obtain an accurate, complete observation of r's actual effect count after b. If the count is zero, CANCELLED is sound: there was no past effect and the barrier excludes future ones. If it is one, return COMMITTED and do not replace. Quiescence alone is insufficient because an effect may have occurred before b without a wrapper record; an accurate zero read alone is insufficient because execution may occur afterward. Eventual availability of both certificate and outcome observation establishes resolution liveness. A genuine known end-to-end bound after which every attempt has either committed or become permanently incapable of committing can supply quiescence, but an ordinary client timeout, queue-only expiry, or worker termination does not prove that bound.

reasoning_steps.argument: As an analytical bridge, define Y_H = 1 when exactly one actual effect has occurred by horizon H, and let Z be the wrapper's completion label. Choose H after replacement and after the delayed original in P, with no downstream notification before H. D and P can have identical wrapper observations and Z, but Y_H is respectively one and zero. Replicating either history over distinct request identities permits all completion labels to agree while the disagreement fraction is respectively zero or one. Thus these observations alone justify no nontrivial whole-cell disagreement budget; this does not challenge a certificate explicitly conditional on a valid budget. Also, Y_H = 1 before a late effect does not establish permanent cancellation safety. This narrows the next step from merely obtaining more correctness judgments to checking authoritative outcome evidence plus exclusion. The next implementation test, when a service and oracle are available, is to pause a dispatched call beyond the wrapper's last token check, obtain local cancellation, acknowledge a replacement, and then release the old call. A true exclusion mechanism must prevent the late original effect; an upstream-only mechanism permits two effects. An evaluator-only actual-effect ledger and a commit-before-barrier control are required. These are predictions and a proposed test, not measured results.

assumptions: For the impossibility result, original and replacement effects are irreversible and additive; each dispatched request executes at most once, distinct requests are not deduplicated, and there are no other writers or compensations.

An already-dispatched original request may be permanently discarded or delayed for an arbitrarily long finite time. Downstream execution does not check wrapper fencing tokens or serialize its effect with wrapper record updates.
No available channel certifies permanent original-request nonexecution. Any available read-only commitment query may accurately report absence while the original remains pending.

The wrapper continues executing with reliable durable local operations. Guarantees range over all admissible downstream schedules; the argument uses deterministic policies or fixes policy randomness when requiring pointwise guarantees.

CANCELLED authorizes replacement only if the original has produced no effect and cannot produce any later. Conclusive resolution means a truthful COMMITTED or sound CANCELLED result, not UNKNOWN, escalation, or mere process termination.

For the separate sufficient participation result only, seal and actual commitment satisfy the durable effect-boundary serialization and terminal exclusion contract. This is not assumed of the original downstream tool.

For the separate sufficient quiescence result only, a trustworthy barrier excludes every future original effect, new wrapper dispatches remain closed, and a complete accurate post-barrier observation establishes whether an original effect occurred.

For liveness under either changed contract, the requisite terminal evidence eventually arrives. Confirmed task completion additionally requires successful processing and acknowledgment of any authorized single replacement.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the evaluation unit and target before scoring
reasoning_steps.argument: For each agent a, freeze a cohort of N_a task executions, including assigned tasks, environment versions, tool access, model and prompt versions, execution budgets, and observation horizon H. Let O_ai be the evaluator's binary acceptance decision. Let Y_ai be reference correctness: the required external postcondition holds at H and all predeclared safety and resource constraints are satisfied. Timeouts and missing required evidence count as failures under this rubric, not discarded runs. Define q_a = N_a^(-1) sum_i O_ai and p_a = N_a^(-1) sum_i Y_ai. These are finite-cohort rates. Correlation among executions does not invalidate their definitions. The binary target should accompany, not replace, separate severity, cost, and recovery reporting.

reasoning_steps.title: Acceptance and correctness differ by two identifiable error components
reasoning_steps.argument: Define f_a = N_a^(-1) sum_i O_ai(1-Y_ai), the fraction of all runs falsely accepted, and n_a = N_a^(-1) sum_i (1-O_ai)Y_ai, the fraction falsely rejected. The pointwise identity Y = O - O(1-Y) + (1-O)Y gives p_a = q_a - f_a + n_a exactly. Therefore p_A-p_B = q_A-q_B-f_A+f_B+n_A-n_B. An acceptance gain can arise from a correctness gain, increased false acceptance, decreased false rejection, or a combination; acceptance alone cannot separate these terms.

reasoning_steps.title: Exact ranking reversal with unchanged evaluator observations
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider 100 equally weighted records per agent, indexed i=1,...,100. Fix O_Ai=1 exactly when i<=90 and O_Bi=1 exactly when i<=80. In World I, set Y_Ai=O_Ai and Y_Bi=O_Bi: correctness is 90% versus 80%. In World II, set Y_Ai=1 exactly when i<=70, leaving Y_Bi=O_Bi: correctness is 70% versus 80%. All observed acceptance labels are identical across worlds; in World II, A has 20 false acceptances and no false rejections. If indices are instead sampled uniformly with replacement, both worlds also induce the same distribution of observed label pairs for every sample size. Thus no estimator using only these observations can consistently distinguish the opposite correctness rankings. Other logs do not help if they omit the distinguishing external reference state; this construction does not claim impossibility when logs actually determine correctness.

reasoning_steps.title: Sharp bounds when evaluator disagreement is bounded
reasoning_steps.argument: Suppose an externally justified bound states that P(O_a != Y_a)<=epsilon_a for a uniformly selected cohort record. Since |p_a-q_a|=|n_a-f_a|<=n_a+f_a, p_a lies in [L_a,U_a]=[max(0,q_a-epsilon_a), min(1,q_a+epsilon_a)]. These bounds are sharp in the unrestricted binary-label model: the lower endpoint is attained by changing min(epsilon_a,q_a) accepted mass into incorrect outcomes, and the upper endpoint by changing min(epsilon_a,1-q_a) rejected mass into correct outcomes. On a finite cohort, use attainable integer counts. Consequently the unrestricted difference interval is [L_A-U_B,U_A-L_B], with both endpoints attainable absent further cross-agent constraints. Strict superiority is certified only if L_A>U_B; a simple sufficient condition is q_A-q_B>epsilon_A+epsilon_B. The inequality is a certificate under a validated error bound, not a reason to assume that bound.

reasoning_steps.title: Estimate the needed errors by auditing both acceptance cells
reasoning_steps.argument: Within each agent, partition the fixed records by O=1 and O=0. Let r_a+ be the fraction with Y=0 in the accepted cell and r_a- the fraction with Y=1 in the rejected cell. Then f_a=q_a r_a+, n_a=(1-q_a)r_a-, and p_a=q_a(1-r_a+)+(1-q_a)r_a-. Uniformly sample records without replacement separately within every nonempty cell, and obtain reference labels independently of the agent's completion claim. An accepted-only audit identifies false acceptance but leaves false rejection unknown. Auditing both cells identifies both terms if the reference labels are accurate. An empty cell has zero weight, so its conditional error rate need not be defined.

reasoning_steps.title: A simultaneous finite-cohort confidence certificate
reasoning_steps.argument: Let K<=4 be the number of nonempty agent-by-acceptance cells for two agents. Prespecify each audit sample size m_c. For a nonexhaustively audited cell, compute its observed binary error fraction rhat_c and t_c=sqrt(log(2K/alpha)/(2m_c)); set l_c=max(0,rhat_c-t_c), u_c=min(1,rhat_c+t_c). Hoeffding's inequality for uniform sampling without replacement bounds each cell's two-sided failure probability by 2 exp(-2m_c t_c^2)=alpha/K. reasoning_steps.title: Define the task, tool contract, and success event
reasoning_steps.argument: The task is to create exactly one irreversible external effect, represented by an integer counter N initially equal to zero. Each executed call to apply(payload) increments N by one; acknowledgments do not reveal N. There is no decrement, cancellation, status query, deduplication, or other observation of N available to the agent. Evaluation occurs at a fixed finite horizon T after recovery terminates. Effect-level success is N=1; truthful completion and safe handling of uncertainty are additional metrics, not substitutes for this condition. Any stronger end-to-end success requirement implies effect-level success, so an upper bound on the latter also bounds the former.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct the indistinguishable failure pair
reasoning_steps.argument: In history H0, the initial request is discarded without execution and the client receives a timeout, leaving N=0. In history H1, the initial request executes, its acknowledgment is lost, and the client receives the same timeout, leaving N=1. The local checkpoint, request bytes, timing observations, and all other agent-visible information are identical. The initial request is quiescent in both histories: it cannot execute later. Every subsequent recovery call, if any, executes once and receives the same generic acknowledgment on the same schedule in both histories. These are two admissible schedules under the stated contract, not claims about their prevalence.

reasoning_steps.title: Adaptive reasoning cannot distinguish these histories
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix the recovery policy's internal random choices, including stochastic model decisions. Initially its observable state is identical in H0 and H1. If its observed histories remain identical through one step, its next action is identical; a wait, local operation, or repeated call then receives an identical observation by construction. Induction therefore gives identical recovery transcripts and the same number R of additional calls. Removing the conditioning on randomness shows that R has the same distribution in both histories. Checkpoint restoration and a fresh agent run do not invalidate this argument if they have only the specified observations and actions.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive the impossibility and tight minimax bound
reasoning_steps.argument: At the horizon, H0 has N=R and H1 has N=1+R. Success in H0 therefore requires R=1, while success in H1 requires R=0. Consequently s0=Pr(R=1) and s1=Pr(R=0), with s0+s1<=1 and min(s0,s1)<=1/2. The effect-level bound is tight: a policy that makes exactly one additional call with probability 1/2 and otherwise makes none achieves success probability 1/2 in each history. Deterministic stopping yields counts (0,1), one retry yields (1,2), and two or more retries fail in both. If the committed history has a known prior probability p, optimal average effect-level success is max(p,1-p); that prior does not provide a guarantee for each history. Abstention can avoid a false completion claim but cannot guarantee task completion.

reasoning_steps.title: Locate the failure propagation and recovery boundary
reasoning_steps.argument: The initiating fault is loss of information about external commitment, not necessarily an incorrect plan or model judgment. It creates uncertainty between N=0 and N=1. Blind retry converts that uncertainty into a duplicate effect in H1; refusing to retry leaves an omission in H0. Restoring local memory does not restore external state. A more capable model or another critic given the same information cannot eliminate this ambiguity. This does not refute recovery in systems with additional observations, reversible effects, or stronger tool contracts; those systems fall outside the construction.

reasoning_steps.title: State a sufficient changed contract rather than a universal remedy
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider instead a tool that accepts a logical-operation key k and immutable payload, atomically couples its effect with a durable record for k, and returns the stored result on every replay. With no other writers, atomic deduplication makes the number of effects for k at most one. If at least one invocation is processed successfully by T, it is also at least one, so N=1. This is a conditional safety-and-completion argument: deduplication alone does not guarantee availability or delivery. Merely attaching a request ID does not establish the contract; an effect followed by a crash before a separate deduplication write still permits duplication.
